title: Act 1: Hobson's World & Maggie's Plan
description: Hobson’s tyranny, the boot shop, Maggie’s proposal, and the daughters’ opening conflict.
content_html:
Act 1: Establishing the World

Act 1 of Hobson’s Choice introduces the central conflict in a single, brilliantly constructed scene. We meet all the key characters, learn the power dynamics of the Hobson household, and witness the moment that sets the entire plot in motion — Maggie’s proposal to Willie Mossop. By the end of the act, the audience understands exactly what is at stake: Hobson’s world is about to be turned upside down.

Hobson’s Tyranny

Henry Horatio Hobson is a prosperous boot-shop owner who rules his household like a petty tyrant. He refuses to pay his three daughters — Maggie, Alice, and Vickey — for the work they do in his shop, declaring that they get their “keep” and should be grateful. He controls when they can go out, who they can see, and whether they can marry. When Alice and Vickey raise the subject of marriage, Hobson dismisses them contemptuously.

Hobson’s authority is presented as absurd from the start. He stumbles in from the Moonraker’s pub, hungover, and lectures his daughters on respectability while being unable to manage his own behaviour. Brighouse uses this dramatic irony to undermine Hobson immediately: the audience sees a man whose authority is built on bluster, not competence. His line “I’m a natural shopkeeper” is laughable — it is Maggie who runs the business and Willie who makes the boots.

Key Fact

Hobson claims authority as a father and businessman but demonstrates neither competence nor moral standing. The audience sees this gap immediately — his daughters do the real work while he drinks at the Moonraker’s.

The Three Daughters

Brighouse carefully differentiates the three Hobson sisters. Alice (the middle daughter) and Vickey (the youngest) are conventional and genteel — they want to marry well and climb the social ladder. Alice is courting Albert Prosser, a solicitor’s son, while Vickey is interested in Fred Beenstock. Both men represent the professional middle class that Alice and Vickey aspire to join.

Maggie, at thirty, is the eldest and considered “on the shelf” by her father. Hobson dismisses her marriage prospects: “you’re shelved.” But Maggie is the most capable person in the shop. She manages the customers, keeps the accounts, and drives the sales. When Mrs Hepworth, a wealthy customer, comes in and demands to know who made her boots, it is Maggie who fetches Willie from the cellar — and Maggie who recognises the significance of Mrs Hepworth’s praise.

Mrs Hepworth’s arrival is a pivotal moment. She is an upper-class customer who has come specifically to find the craftsman who made her boots. She tells Willie: “You’re a natural born genius at making boots.” This is the first time anyone has recognised Willie’s talent. Crucially, Mrs Hepworth gives Willie her calling card and tells him to contact her if he ever leaves Hobson’s. This plants the seed for the entire plot — Maggie sees that Willie has a marketable skill that Hobson is exploiting for pennies.

Mrs Hepworth also represents the world beyond the shop — a world of wealth and discernment that values quality. Her recognition of Willie is the evidence Maggie needs to justify her plan.

Maggie’s Proposal to Willie

The most dramatic moment in Act 1 is Maggie’s proposal to Willie Mossop. This reverses every Victorian convention: the woman proposes to the man; the employer’s daughter proposes to the cellar worker; the older, educated woman proposes to the timid, barely literate craftsman. “I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll take Willie Mossop” is one of the most important lines in the play — it announces Maggie’s absolute agency.

Willie is terrified. He protests that he is already “tokened” (engaged) to Ada Figgins, and that marrying above his station is unthinkable. But Maggie is relentless. She sees what nobody else does: Willie’s extraordinary talent with boots, combined with her business brain, can build something far greater than Hobson’s shop. Her proposal is not romantic — it is a business proposition. “I’m a business woman” she declares, making it clear that this marriage is built on partnership and mutual advantage.

Key Fact

“I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll take Willie Mossop” — Maggie’s proposal reverses Victorian gender norms. She is the active agent, choosing her own husband based on practical ability rather than romance or social status.

Willie’s initial resistance is significant. He is not being modest — he genuinely believes he is too low in the social hierarchy to marry an employer’s daughter. His world view has been shaped by the class system: certain things are simply “not done.” When Ada Figgins and her mother arrive to defend Ada’s claim on Willie, the scene becomes a comic battle for possession of a man who barely speaks. Ada physically grabs Willie; Maggie calmly removes her. The comedy underscores a serious point: Willie is treated as property by everyone — by Hobson, by Ada, and even initially by Maggie. His journey through the play is about becoming a person who makes his own choices.

Hobson’s Reaction

When Hobson learns of Maggie’s plan, he is outraged. He reaches for his belt to beat Willie — a physical expression of patriarchal authority. But Maggie intercepts: she tells Willie that if Hobson strikes him, they will leave immediately. This is the first direct challenge to Hobson’s power, and he does not know how to respond. The belt remains the symbol of his authority, and when he uses it, he inadvertently gives Maggie the justification to leave with Willie. Hobson’s violence is what propels the plot forward.
exam_tip_html: The Edexcel question gives you a short quotation and asks you to write about the whole play. If the quotation is from Act 1, start your analysis there but range across all four acts. Show how Act 1 sets up conflicts and ideas that develop later. For example, Maggie’s proposal in Act 1 leads directly to her triumph in Act 4 — trace this arc to demonstrate your knowledge of the whole text.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Act 1 establishes Hobson as a blundering tyrant whose authority is built on bluster, not competence — the audience sees the gap between his self-image and reality.
  • Maggie’s proposal to Willie reverses Victorian gender conventions: she chooses her own husband based on his skill, declaring “I’m a business woman.”
  • Mrs Hepworth’s recognition of Willie’s talent (“natural born genius”) provides the evidence Maggie needs to justify her plan and sets the plot in motion.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse present Hobson as an ineffective authority figure in Act 1? You should consider the context in which the play was written.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive analysis of Hobson’s gap between self-image and reality. Discusses: his hangover entrance, his refusal to pay his daughters, his claim to be a ‘natural shopkeeper’ while relying on Maggie and Willie, the belt as a symbol of failing authority. Embeds patriarchal control, Victorian father’s legal authority. Brighouse’s use of dramatic irony and comedy.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Brighouse uses Maggie’s proposal to Willie Mossop to challenge Victorian expectations about gender and class.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive exploration of the double reversal (gender + class). Discusses: woman proposing to a man, employer’s daughter choosing a cellar worker, the business logic of the proposal (‘I’m a business woman’), Willie’s reluctance reflecting internalised class boundaries. Victorian marriage conventions, Married Women’s Property Acts. Brighouse’s use of comedy to normalise radical ideas.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with embedded context.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse use the character of Mrs Hepworth to advance the plot and introduce the theme of meritocracy in Act 1?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive analysis of Mrs Hepworth as a catalyst. Discusses: her recognition of Willie’s talent (‘natural born genius’), the calling card as a plot device, her upper-class status validating Willie’s skill across class boundaries, and how Maggie uses this evidence. Victorian meritocracy vs inherited status.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with textual support.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: “In Act 1, Brighouse shows us that the real power in Hobson’s shop belongs to the women.” How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Convincing argument. Agrees: Maggie runs sales, manages customers, drives the business; Alice and Vickey handle the shop floor. But complicates: Hobson still has legal authority as father and property owner; the daughters are unpaid; Maggie’s power is unofficial. Concludes: women have practical power but not formal authority, which is precisely what Maggie seeks to change.
Top band (16-20): Balanced argument with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some engagement with the statement.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited discussion.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Brighouse contrasts Maggie with her sisters Alice and Vickey in Act 1. What does this contrast reveal about different attitudes to women’s roles?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive comparison. Discusses: Alice and Vickey seeking respectable marriages (conventional route), Maggie choosing a partner based on skill (unconventional), the sisters’ concern with fashion and appearance vs Maggie’s practicality. different models of womanhood available in 1880s society. Brighouse’s use of foil characters.
Top band (16-20): Clear comparison with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant contrasts.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse create comedy in Act 1, and what is the purpose of the humour?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive analysis of comedy as a vehicle for social critique. Discusses: Hobson’s pompous speeches undercut by his hungover state, the Ada Figgins scene as physical comedy, Willie’s bewilderment, Maggie’s dry wit. dramatic irony, comic timing, comedy of manners. Purpose: humour makes the audience sympathise with Maggie and Willie while seeing Hobson’s authority as ridiculous.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion of comic techniques.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

glossary_terms.definition: An absolute ruler who exercises power oppressively and without regard for others’ wishes or wellbeing.
Comedy that arises from the gap between how a character sees themselves and how the audience perceives them.
Concerned with what is socially acceptable and respectable, often at the expense of genuine feeling or independent thought.
The ability to act independently and make one’s own choices, rather than being controlled by external forces or other people.
The exercise of power and control by a dominant figure, typically a father or male authority, over those considered subordinate.
